title: 3 Critical Guidelines For Enforcing Class Rules
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recounts a distressing conversation with a student who was ready to give up on school after a teacher wrongly accused him of breaking a rule and refused to hear him out. He extracts three guidelines for enforcing rules fairly: let misbehavior fully play out and confirm it actually occurred before stepping in, rather than reacting on assumption; acknowledge that teachers will occasionally get it wrong and commit in advance to correcting mistakes, including apologizing in front of the class when warranted; and always afford students basic respect, including the right to be heard, regardless of prior history. He closes by emphasizing that firm, consistent enforcement of rules must be paired with genuine compassion and humility about teachers' own fallibility.
points: Opens with a real account of a student nearly disengaging from school after being wrongly accused and denied the chance to explain.
Guideline one: let misbehavior fully play out and confirm it before enforcing a consequence, to avoid false accusations.
Guideline two: promise students in advance that teacher mistakes will be corrected, including public apology when warranted.
Guideline three: always afford students basic respect and the right to be heard, regardless of their disciplinary history.
Closes by arguing that firm, consistent rule enforcement must be paired with genuine compassion, humility, and empathy for students' inner lives.
quotes: Sadly, it all could have been avoided if the teacher would have followed three simple but critical guidelines for enforcing class rules.
It’s imperative that you get it right, that you know a rule has been broken before stepping in with a consequence.
When first teaching your classroom management plan, promise your students that if you ever make a mistake, which is a real possibility, you’ll fix it.
What he was absolutely furious about, however, almost inconsolable, was that she refused to give him a voice.
We use our own memories of those teachers who slighted us or were outright cruel to us as well as the guardian angels who had a kind word and soft heart at the moment we most needed it.
